body.text: The process of experimentation is the core requirement of the federal R&D tax credit under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) for U.S. taxpayers. Substantially all (at least 80%) of a business component's activities must systematically identify technical uncertainty, formulate alternatives, and evaluate them through modeling, simulation, or trial and error, backed by contemporaneous documentation.
Executive Summary: Statutory Mandate and Evidentiary Function of the Process of Experimentation

The Process of Experimentation (POE) constitutes the core procedural requirement under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 and its governing Treasury Regulations for establishing qualified research activities eligible for the United States federal research and development (R&D) tax credit. Operating as an essential pillar of the statutory four-part test codified in IRC § 41(d), the POE mandate under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) dictates that "substantially all" of a taxpayer's activities aimed at developing or improving a business component must comprise elements of a systematic process of experimentation related to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality. Rather than rewarding general technical complexity, professional engineering competence, or commercial problem-solving, this statutory mandate functions as a rigorous legal filter that confines tax credit eligibility to structured, scientific inquiry designed to resolve genuine technological unknowns.

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5) operationalizes this statutory standard by requiring a demonstrable, systematic protocol structured around three sequential steps: identifying the specific technical uncertainty concerning capability, method, or appropriate design at the outset of research activities; identifying one or more alternative solutions intended to eliminate that uncertainty; and systematically conducting an evaluation of those alternatives through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error approach. In both Internal Revenue Service (IRS) examinations and United States Tax Court litigation, the POE serves as the primary qualitative and quantitative threshold separating qualified research from routine engineering, standard design adaptation, regulatory data compilation, and commercial production activities.

Judicial scrutiny in decisions including Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2024-113), Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)), and Moore v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-20) confirms that the POE is fundamentally an evidentiary standard. Taxpayers cannot substantiate a POE merely by demonstrating that a project was technically challenging or resulted in revised drawings or functional software code; rather, contemporaneous documentation must explicitly record how and why specific technical alternatives were formulated, tested, and iteratively modified to eliminate defined technical uncertainties. Concurrently, administrative enforcement initiatives launched under IRS News Release IR-2021-203 (effective for refund claims filed after January 10, 2022, and subsequently refined in June 2024) and expanded business component reporting under Section G of revised Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) compel taxpayers to integrate POE substantiation directly into their operational engineering and software development lifecycles prior to return filing.

The convergence of strict judicial interpretation under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6) and upfront administrative reporting on Form 6765 transforms the POE from a substantive engineering criterion into a strict accounting segregation requirement. Because the 80% "substantially all" threshold under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) operates as an all-or-nothing cliff at the defined business component level, a failure to contemporaneously separate routine design adaptation hours from experimental evaluation hours does not merely reduce a taxpayer's credit proportionally—it invalidates 100% of the qualified research expenses (QREs) associated with that business component unless the taxpayer has preserved sufficient subcomponent accounting granularity to invoke the shrink-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2).
Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of the Process of Experimentation
Placement Within the IRC Section 41(d) Four-Part Test

Eligibility for the federal research credit under IRC § 41 requires a taxpayer to satisfy a cumulative four-part statutory test applied separately to each discrete business component. While pedagogical frameworks variably sequence the POE as either the third or fourth component in conceptual summaries, the statutory architecture of IRC § 41(d)(1) integrates four distinct legal prerequisites that operate in tandem and must all be satisfied concurrently.

First, under the Section 174 Expense and Technological Uncertainty Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3), the expenditures must qualify as research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174, requiring that information available to the taxpayer at the outset does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of that component. Second, under the Technological in Nature Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4), the activity must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the Permitted Purpose Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(3)(A), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information whose application is intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality. Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5), substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to that qualified purpose.

Within this statutory architecture, the POE acts as the procedural nexus connecting the taxpayer's foundational scientific discipline (Technological in Nature) and objective technical goal (Permitted Purpose) to the actual resolution of the underlying technical unknown (Technological Uncertainty). Whereas the Technological in Nature and Permitted Purpose tests evaluate static attributes of a project—whether the domain involves hard sciences and whether the target outcome is functional improvement—the POE test scrutinizes the dynamic evaluation protocol executed by the taxpayer's personnel across the project lifecycle. If a taxpayer fails to substantiate the systematic evaluation mechanics of the POE for a given business component, the entire claim associated with that component is invalidated regardless of whether the project relied on advanced engineering principles or sought to improve product performance.

An analytical compliance framework assigns 50% of the overall audit substantiation difficulty weight to the Process of Experimentation alone, compared to 20% for Elimination of Uncertainty, 15% for Permitted Purpose, and 15% for Technological in Nature. That same pedagogical model contrasts a qualified experimental process—scoring 90 on technical uncertainty, 95 on documented alternatives, and 85 on audit survival rate—against a routine debugging fix scoring 20, 10, and 15 across those respective dimensions, while citing an illustrative heuristic that "80% of disallowed claims fail due to lack of substantiated experimentation" (a pedagogical benchmark rather than an official IRS empirical audit statistic, distinct from the statutory 80% "substantially all" rule in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)).

body.text: Deconstructing the Three-Pronged Regulatory Framework Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(5)

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) defines a process of experimentation as a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. The regulatory standard requires that the taxpayer's activities satisfy three sequential, interdependent structural prongs.

Under the first prong (Identification of Technical Uncertainty), the research activity must begin by explicitly identifying the technical uncertainty regarding the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of that business component. This requirement anchors the project in genuine technological discovery rather than the routine application of existing engineering or scientific knowledge. A critical causal relationship governs the interaction between Prong 1 and the subsequent prongs: if the initial uncertainty is framed around commercial viability, cost estimation, aesthetic preference, or scheduling constraints rather than technical capability, method, or design, any subsequent evaluation of alternatives automatically fails to constitute a qualified POE because the alternatives are not resolving a Section 174 technological uncertainty.

Under the second prong (Identification of Alternatives), subsequent to defining the baseline uncertainty, the taxpayer must formulate and identify one or more specific technical alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty. Where a single standard solution can be selected immediately from established industry knowledge, technical manuals, building codes, or vendor specifications, the formulation of experimental alternatives is absent and the activity fails the POE threshold.

Under the third prong (Systematic Conduct and Evaluation), the taxpayer must execute a structured process of evaluating the identified alternatives through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error approach. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) explicitly recognizes that a process of experimentation may operate as a sequential design process—where a single alternative is tested, analyzed, and iteratively refined based on test results—or as a concurrent evaluation of multiple competing alternatives, provided the evaluation systematically tests hypotheses, analyzes resulting data, and informs subsequent design iterations.

cells: Define the capability, method, or appropriate design not determinable from available information at project outset.
Asserting commercial, financial, aesthetic, or scheduling uncertainty rather than technical uncertainty.
Formulate and record one or more distinct technical solutions intended to resolve the defined uncertainty.
Selecting a known off-the-shelf configuration or applying a routine fix without evaluating competing options.
Execute structured testing, computer modeling, simulation, or systematic trial-and-error to validate or reject alternatives.
Empirical or Theoretical Resolution of Uncertainty
Issuing revised drawings or code via unstructured tinkering or generic design phases without linking test data to design revisions.

body.text: The Substantially All Mandate and Methodological Neutrality Toward Project Outcomes

IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) imposes a quantitative gatekeeper on the POE by requiring that "substantially all" of the activities related to a business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "substantially all" requirement is satisfied only if 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities for the business component—measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, such as employee labor hours—constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose.

This statutory threshold prevents taxpayers from claiming the research credit across the entire cost pool of a broad commercial project when only an isolated fraction of the labor involved genuine experimentation. When a project's total labor hours are heavily diluted by routine drafting, administrative project management, standard quality control, or commercial adaptation, the aggregate activities for that business component fall below the 80% threshold and fail IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) in their entirety unless the taxpayer can isolate a smaller, discrete subsystem under the "shrink-back" rule of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2).

To illustrate the exact mathematical mechanics of the "substantially all" threshold under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) alongside the shrink-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), consider an engineering firm that undertakes the development of a custom laboratory environmental control system (Business Component A) requiring 1,000 hours at a uniform wage rate of $100/hour, representing $100,000 in total wage expenditures. At the whole-system level, employee time logs document 100 hours ($10,000) devoted to Prong 1 activities (defining airflow pressure-drop and thermal recovery uncertainties), 150 hours ($15,000) devoted to Prong 2 activities (formulating three alternative variable-air-volume actuator control designs), and 450 hours ($45,000) devoted to Prong 3 activities (computational fluid dynamics simulation and empirical bench testing of the three alternatives), alongside 300 hours ($30,000) spent on non-experimental activities comprising routine building code verification, standard ductwork CAD drafting, and general project administration. Summing the three experimental prongs yields the total POE hours and activity ratio at the whole-system level:
Total POE Hours<sub>Whole-System</sub> = 100 hours + 150 hours + 450 hours = 700 hours (or $70,000)
POE Activity Ratio<sub>Whole-System</sub> = 700 hours ÷ 1,000 hours = 70.0%

Because 70.0% < 80.0%, Business Component A fails the "substantially all" requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) at the whole-system level, disqualifying the entire $100,000 wage pool if claimed as a single business component. However, if the taxpayer applies the shrink-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to narrow the business component definition to the discrete variable-air-volume actuator subsystem (Subcomponent A-1), which consumed 500 hours ($50,000)—comprising 425 hours ($42,500) of direct Prong 1–3 experimentation and 75 hours ($7,500) of routine subsystem integration—the activity ratio is recomputed as follows:
POE Activity Ratio<sub>Subcomponent A-1</sub> = 425 hours ÷ 500 hours = 85.0%

Because 85.0% ≥ 80.0%, Subcomponent A-1 satisfies the "substantially all" standard, qualifying the discrete subsystem for the credit. This mathematical bifurcation highlights a vital operational reality: the shrink-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) is legally unavailable in practice if the taxpayer's time-tracking system records labor only at the macro project level ("Business Component A"), because neither the taxpayer nor the examining agent can isolate the denominator (500 hours) or numerator (425 hours) of Subcomponent A-1 without subcomponent-level accounting records.

Crucially, the legal evaluation of the POE is strictly methodological rather than outcome-dependent. Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) and § 1.41-4(a)(5) establish that eligibility turns entirely on whether the taxpayer executed the structured three-pronged process to resolve technical uncertainty, regardless of whether the resulting design succeeds or fails commercially or technically. Indeed, documented test failures often serve as the strongest empirical proof in an IRS examination or Tax Court proceeding that genuine technical uncertainty existed at the outset and that multiple alternatives required systematic evaluation. Conversely, a project that achieves commercial deployment on its first design pass without failed iterations or comparative modeling creates a strong evidentiary presumption that the appropriate design was already knowable from available engineering principles.
Judicial Precedent Defining Systematic Evaluation Versus Routine Professional Competence
Distinguishing Exploratory Experimentation from Routine Adaptation and Code Compliance

Federal courts have repeatedly enforced a sharp boundary between exploratory scientific experimentation and the routine application of professional competence in engineering, architecture, and manufacturing. Satisfying mandatory regulatory or industry standards—such as designing building systems to comply with local building, fire, or energy codes—does not establish a qualified process of experimentation when the engineer achieves compliance by applying known calculations and standard engineering approaches.

Similarly, adhering to structured commercial workflows, such as the standard American Institute of Architects (AIA) design phases (schematic design, design development, construction documents, and bidding or negotiation), does not inherently constitute a POE under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C). While professional design phases involve iterative client feedback, interdisciplinary coordination, and progressive drawing refinement, they fail the statutory standard unless the taxpayer proves with specific records that the revisions resulted from systematically testing competing technical alternatives to overcome a capability, method, or design uncertainty.
Evidentiary Deficiencies in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner

The United States Tax Court's memorandum opinion in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Docket No. 4049-19, decided December 19, 2024), illustrates the fatal consequences of conflating complex professional engineering with a statutory Process of Experimentation. Phoenix Design Group, Inc. (PDG), a multidisciplinary consulting firm specializing in mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) engineering for commercial and institutional buildings, claimed R&D tax credits across numerous design projects. The Tax Court disallowed 100% of the claimed credits, holding that PDG failed to prove that "substantially all" of its project activities constituted elements of a systematic process of experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6).

Three primary evidentiary failures drove the Tax Court's holding in Phoenix Design Group. First, the record suffered from unexplained design revisions: although PDG produced project documentation showing that engineers revised designs and issued multiple rounds of updated drawings (such as designing a custom HVAC system for a laboratory facility), the firm provided "no explanation of why or how these revisions addressed uncertainties" through a systematic evaluation of alternatives. Iterative drawing revisions triggered by client scope changes, architectural coordination, or budget adjustments do not constitute scientific experimentation.

Second, the court found that the disputed engineering tasks constituted "routine design adaptations" rather than experimental hypothesis testing, as sizing equipment, performing standard load calculations, and configuring building systems to fit site-specific spatial constraints are inherent to standard MEPF engineering practice. Third, PDG employees recorded labor hours using broad, "generic narratives" (such as general project phase descriptions) that failed to link specific hours worked to the resolution of defined technical uncertainties or the evaluation of distinct alternatives. Because the taxpayer could not substantiate which specific hours involved qualifying experimentation versus routine engineering, it could not meet its burden of proving that at least 80% ("substantially all") of the activities on any business component satisfied the POE standard.
Corroborating Precedent in Little Sandy Coal and Moore

The evidentiary posture established in Phoenix Design Group builds directly upon earlier judicial holdings in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15 (aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)), and Moore v. Commissioner (Scott Moore), T.C. Memo. 2023-20 (decided February 23, 2023). In Little Sandy Coal, a shipbuilder sought R&D tax credits for designing and constructing a tank barge and a dry dock. Both the Tax Court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit sustained the disallowance of the credits because the taxpayer lacked contemporaneous documentation quantifying the proportion of employee and production activities dedicated to a process of experimentation, rendering the court unable to verify that the 80% "substantially all" threshold of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) was met. Similarly, in Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20, the Tax Court rejected credit claims involving executive compensation where the taxpayer relied on retrospective testimony and lacked contemporaneous records linking specific activities and time spent to a structured process of experimentation.

Taken together, Little Sandy Coal, Moore, and Phoenix Design Group establish an unforgiving judicial doctrine: even where a project involves novel engineering elements, courts refuse to apply judicial estimation (such as the Cohan rule) to salvage the 80% "substantially all" fraction under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) when the taxpayer's underlying time records blend routine professional services with experimental testing. Furthermore, Phoenix Design Group demonstrates that preserving versioned artifacts (such as sequential CAD drawing sets) without preserving the intermediate analytical link—the documented test result or simulation failure that forced the transition from Version A to Version B—leaves the taxpayer vulnerable to a judicial finding that the versions merely reflect routine design development.

body.text: Practical Qualification Benchmarks Across Theoretical and Empirical Approaches

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) explicitly recognizes that the systematic evaluation of alternatives (Prong 3) may be executed through either theoretical protocols—such as computer modeling and numerical simulation—or empirical protocols involving physical prototyping and systematic trial-and-error testing.
Iterative Theoretical Experimentation via Modeling and Simulation

When constructing physical prototypes is cost-prohibitive or technically impractical during early-stage development, taxpayers satisfy the POE requirement through iterative theoretical modeling and simulation. In this approach, engineers construct mathematical or computer-aided models to test how alternative design parameters behave under simulated physical conditions, using the output data to incrementally revise the design until the technical uncertainty is eliminated.

Consider a textile manufacturer developing a lightweight, thermally insulated tote bag where the optimal ratio of insulation volume to structural weight is unknown at the outset of development (Prong 1). The engineering team formulates several candidate material geometries and insulation thicknesses (Prong 2) and uses computer-assisted design (CAD) and thermal modeling software to simulate heat transfer rates and weight distributions across each virtual prototype (Prong 3). By systematically analyzing the simulated thermal performance metrics and iteratively modifying the CAD geometry until the target thermal-to-weight specification is achieved, the engineering team executes a qualified theoretical POE under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5). Note the critical distinction between this textile modeling scenario and the disallowed HVAC design work in Phoenix Design Group: in the qualifying scenario, CAD software is coupled with thermal simulation to test competing material-geometry hypotheses against an unknown performance trade-off, whereas in Phoenix Design Group, CAD software was used primarily to record site-adapted layouts without documented comparative simulation of uncertain designs.
Empirical Systematic Trial-and-Error in Software Development

In software engineering and physical product fabrication, the POE frequently takes the form of empirical, systematic trial-and-error. Crucially, regulatory compliance requires that trial-and-error be systematic—meaning that each test iteration is driven by an explicit hypothesis, evaluated against measurable performance criteria, and used to direct the next modification—rather than unstructured "tinkering" or ad-hoc debugging.

Two distinct software engineering scenarios delineate qualified empirical experimentation from routine software maintenance. In the first scenario, involving user interface (UI) functional optimization, a software developer seeks to re-architect a web application's UI to minimize the number of sequential customer clicks required to complete an order transaction, where the appropriate interaction design to achieve that functional latency reduction is uncertain at the outset (Prong 1). The developer formulates alternative UI workflow layouts (Prong 2), deploys the candidate builds, systematically captures empirical user-interaction telemetry, and iteratively revises the UI architecture based on quantitative click-path analysis until the functional uncertainty is resolved (Prong 3).

In the second scenario, contrasting database query latency resolution against routine debugging, a software engineering team confronting severe database query latency (Prong 1) formulates three distinct architectural hypotheses—database indexing versus distributed caching versus a fundamental schema rewrite (Prong 2)—and benchmarks the latency impact of each alternative, documenting that the schema rewrite failed performance targets while the caching architecture succeeded (Prong 3), thereby satisfying the POE standard. Conversely, if a developer encounters a software error, searches the error string online, and applies an established patch from a public repository such as StackOverflow to resolve the bug immediately, the activity is disallowed as a routine fix lacking both methodological uncertainty and the systematic evaluation of alternatives.

body.text: Statutory and Administrative Exclusions from the Process of Experimentation

Both IRC § 41(d)(4) and IRS audit guidelines expressly exclude activities that may occur alongside product development but do not contribute to the scientific resolution of technical uncertainty. Time and expenses incurred solely to organize, format, and compile finalized technical data for mandatory regulatory submissions—such as filings with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)—are excluded from qualified research. As detailed in the IRS Pharmaceutical Industry Research Credit Audit Guidelines (Revised April 30, 2004), administrative data compilation represents post-research documentation organization rather than a scientific or technological contribution to the process of experimentation.

Similarly, pursuant to IRC § 41(d)(4)(D), efficiency surveys, management studies, consumer surveys, market research, and activities related to advertising or promotional testing are statutorily excluded because they address commercial or aesthetic preferences rather than technological uncertainty. Furthermore, making routine design choices or selecting among known vendor components based on price, availability, or standard engineering tables without conducting a documented, systematic evaluation of technical alternatives fails to satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5).
Administrative Disclosure Standards and Contemporaneous Documentation Frameworks
Upfront Substantiation Under IR-2021-203 and Revised Form 6765

The convergence of adverse Tax Court rulings and heightened administrative enforcement has shifted R&D tax credit compliance from retrospective narrative reconstruction to mandatory upfront disclosure. On October 15, 2021, the IRS issued News Release IR-2021-203 (implementing Chief Counsel Advice CCA 20214101F), establishing strict specificity requirements for research credit refund claims filed after January 10, 2022. Under IR-2021-203 as originally issued, a valid claim for refund under IRC § 41 required taxpayers at the time of filing to identify all business components to which the research credit claim related for that tax year, and for each business component, to identify all research activities performed, all individuals who performed each research activity, and the specific information each individual sought to discover.

Administrative guidance subsequently evolved in June 2024 when the IRS waived the requirement on amended refund claims to list the specific names of each individual and the specific information each individual sought to discover at initial filing, while extending the administrative transition period through January 10, 2026. Simultaneously, the IRS released the revised Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities), introducing Section G (Business Component Information—optional for tax year 2024 and mandatory starting tax year 2025 for applicable taxpayers), which codifies component-by-component reporting of research activities and qualified wages directly on original and amended returns. Consequently, substantiating the discrete business component and its underlying Process of Experimentation at the time of return filing remains a binding administrative mandate.
Operationalizing the IRS Compliance Inquiries Through Contemporaneous Artifacts

In examination practice, IRS engineers and examiners distill the statutory requirements of IRC § 41 into three core evidentiary inquiries: identifying what was developed or improved (defining the discrete business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)); demonstrating why the activity is qualified (proving the four-part test, anchored by the technical uncertainty and the three-pronged Process of Experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)); and quantifying how much the qualified activity cost (linking specific QREs to the qualifying experimentation activities and verifying the 80% "substantially all" threshold under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)).

Satisfying the qualification and cost-linkage inquiries requires contemporaneous documentation generated organically during the development lifecycle rather than retroactive interviews conducted years after the tax year closes. The compliance scoring framework evaluates audit readiness across five core operational artifact categories, assigning specific evidentiary weights to each based on its ability to substantiate the three prongs of the POE and grouping cumulative scores into three audit risk tiers: 0%–29% High Risk, 30%–69% Moderate Risk, and 70%–100% Defensive (representing a pedagogical compliance model rather than an official IRS scoring formula).

Within this model, test logs and failure reports carry the highest evidentiary weight at 30%, as empirical test data, simulation outputs, and failed prototype logs directly prove Prong 2 (evaluation of alternatives) and Prong 3 (systematic testing and analysis). Project plans and technical roadmaps account for 20% of the score by establishing Prong 1 at project inception, demonstrating that existing knowledge was insufficient to achieve the target capability, method, or design. Git commit histories and CAD revision logs represent another 20% of the score by tracking the chronological sequence of iterative code or geometry changes over time, bridging test results to specific design modifications when paired with explanatory revision notes. Finally, technical meeting minutes (15% weight) and technical email correspondence (15% weight) provide corroborating contemporaneous evidence by recording engineering design reviews, architectural debates regarding competing solutions, and real-time problem-solving threads discussing how to resolve unforeseen technical bottlenecks during development.

Notice the mathematical implication of this weighting distribution: a taxpayer that retains only project plans (20%) and unannotated Git commits or CAD revision logs (20%) achieves a cumulative score of only 40% (Moderate Risk), which mirrors the exact evidentiary failure in Phoenix Design Group, where the taxpayer had design drawings and project scopes but lacked the test logs, failure reports, and technical review rationales needed to prove why and how the revisions resolved technical uncertainty.

body.text: Compliance Optimization and Regulatory Clarification Strategies
Internal Workflow Architecture for Defensible Experimentation Tracking

To mitigate the exact documentation vulnerabilities that resulted in total credit disallowance in Phoenix Design Group, Little Sandy Coal, and Moore, taxpayers claiming credits under IRC § 41 must implement structural modifications to their internal R&D governance. At the inception of any project intended for the R&D tax credit, technical leads should mandate formal project charters and uncertainty logs to substantiate Prongs 1 and 2. These inception records must explicitly state why existing publicly available information, vendor specifications, or internal know-how cannot establish the capability, method, or appropriate design of the component (Prong 1) and enumerate the specific alternative architectures or formulations scheduled for evaluation (Prong 2).

Furthermore, because standard accounting timecards that log hours to high-level client billing codes or generic project phases ("Design Development", "CAD Drafting", or "Project Engineering") fail the judicial scrutiny applied in Phoenix Design Group, taxpayers must deploy granular activity and uncertainty-linked time tracking to substantiate the 80% "substantially all" standard. Configuring time-tracking and issue-tracking platforms (such as Agile sprint boards or engineering ERP modules) so that employees tag labor hours directly to the specific subcomponent, the technical uncertainty being investigated, or the specific experimental alternative being tested (Prong 3) cleanly segregates qualifying experimentation from non-qualifying routine adaptation and administrative tasks while preserving subcomponent denominators for the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) shrink-back rule. Finally, whenever a design drawing is revised, a CAD model is updated, or a software branch is merged following performance testing, engineers should execute formal iteration and revision memoranda explaining why the prior iteration failed or underperformed during testing, how the empirical data or simulation results dictated the specific modification, and which alternative was validated or discarded.
Policy Frameworks for Administrative Guidance on Iterative Approaches

From a tax administration perspective, ongoing litigation over the boundaries of the POE highlights two critical areas where formal technical guidance from the Treasury Department and the IRS—via updated Audit Technique Guides (ATGs), Revenue Rulings, or safe-harbor procedures—would reduce compliance friction and judicial disputes. First, in applied engineering, architecture, and custom manufacturing, the boundary between site-specific "routine design adaptation" and genuine experimentation remains heavily contested, creating an urgent need for updated industry-specific ATGs that provide concrete examples of qualifying versus non-qualifying engineering iterations. Second, because Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5) was drafted primarily around traditional sequential engineering models, whereas modern software and technology development relies on rapid, iterative Agile sprints and DevOps pipelines, formal administrative safe-harbor guidance is needed to codify how automated unit and integration test suites, sprint backlog tickets, and pull-request failure logs satisfy the three prongs of "systematic trial-and-error" when tracking the resolution of underlying technical uncertainties.

Reduces administrative ambiguity and litigation volume over what constitutes "systematic trial-and-error" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5).

body.text: Conclusion

The Process of Experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5) operates as the decisive legal and evidentiary filter governing federal R&D tax credit eligibility. While taxpayers frequently satisfy the foundational requirements that an activity rely on hard science or engineering (Technological in Nature) and aim toward functional improvement (Permitted Purpose), recent appellate and Tax Court jurisprudence—culminating in Little Sandy Coal, Moore, and Phoenix Design Group—demonstrates that claims routinely collapse when taxpayers cannot prove that at least 80% of their business component activities followed a structured, three-pronged evaluation of technical alternatives. To survive examination under the heightened reporting regime of revised Form 6765 Section G and the specificity standards descended from IR-2021-203, R&D organizations must replace retrospective narrative studies and generic phase-based timecards with prospective uncertainty logs, subcomponent-level time accounting capable of supporting the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) shrink-back rule, and contemporaneous test-to-revision documentation.
